properties.label: Herbalista
properties.description: Herbalista recognizes healthcare as a fundamental human right. We believe that herbal and food-based therapies are foundational to human health and deserve a prominent place at the table. Their mission is to provide the tools, the encouragement, and the lived examples of how we can create that healthier world together. We do this by sponsoring free community health services and education, sharing our Herbalista Model of Care in person and with the greater community, via the web. They also run the 'Grow-a-Row' Program, an herbal garden and learning space in the Summerhill neighborhood of Atlanta "The stewardship goals of this space are to continue the project as a learning garden. When I was getting into gardening and farming, it was kind of intimidating and I had all this uncertainty about how its done. Theres all this conflicting information from books and online, and once I found people who I could garden with, it just made much more sense to me when I was learning with my hands. [So] to have a space where people can get their hands dirty, to have that place to be able to garden and interact with different plants... because everybody deserves that....[Also] a lot of these plants, we can divide and save seeds from, take cuttings from, and so this can be a source for all these other plants to be propagated and spread out into this eco region...for me is the idea of this being like a mother." [Tim Hayes] Tim Hayes, the steward of Herbalista's 'Grow-a-Row' herbal 'mother' garden ,speaks about the value of growing native plants for food, medicine, and even as food for other insects and animals in our local ecosystem. Having more places where people can interact, share knowledge about plants, learn to grow their own food and medicine, take seeds and cuttings to propagate at home, and build community and deeper connection to plants is his mission for the space. 'I want my relationship with plants to be deeper than me just trying to keep a large group of them sort of alive enough for me to get harvest. And so I think growing on a smaller scale and encouraging other people to grow their own food and build that relationship with plants is a big goal of mine...it's fun to me to have a smaller pocket garden and to be interacting with people that are trying to grow their own food or grow their own medicine, or even just grow stuff for the birds and bees. It really feeds my soul...' [Tim Hayes]

properties.label: Ke'nekt Cooperative
properties.description: The Ke'nekt Cooperative is a caf' in Southwest Atlanta, identifying as a Black-liberated third space. The Ke'nekt was born out of a statistic we've known to be true in Atlanta for a while: large infrastructure projects and economic engines like the Beltline have accelerated not just residential gentrification and displacement, but also the displacement of legacy Black businesses. If there is such a thing as economic genocide, it is happening as we speak, and is being furthered by the economic impacts of a global pandemic that is disproportionately affecting Black folks.. The result is a loss of economic, political, and cultural power for Black communities.The Ke'nekt Cooperative was born to repair and remediate this loss. Through collective action and shared cooperative principles, we are creating an economic empowerment ecosystem that fosters ownership, sustainability, and generational wealth. By prioritizing equitable access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making, we aim to break cycles of economic exclusion and build a thriving, self-sufficient community where prosperity is shared, not concentrated. Our work is driven by the belief that economic justice is the foundation for true empowerment, and together, we are reshaping the landscape of commercial real estate to reflect our values of unity, equity, and resilience.

properties.label: The Conservation Fund
properties.description: The Conservation Fund is a national funder that was founded on the idea that environmental protection and economic vitality are mutually reinforcing strategies that make our society stronger. They are twin pillars of a national strategy: economic growth without environmental protection is unsustainable, and environmental protection without economic growth is equally unsustainable. For more than 40 years, The Conservation Fund has been buying at-risk land with high conservation value to protect it from degradation, putting protections in place to ensure it is managed for environmental, economic, and human gain before finding long-term owners. We have worked across all 50 states to conserve more than 9 million acres of irreplaceable American landscapes ' protecting habitat for countless species, supporting millions of jobs, and providing communities across the country with better quality of life. This critical work uniquely positions The Conservation Fund to tackle some of our country's greatest challenges ' from climate solutions, to wildlife protection, to rural economic development, and even access to fresh and healthy food. Our work in conservation is about more than protecting special places, it's also about ensuring that those places will always be healthy, vibrant, and productive contributors to a large and resilient society. 'The Conservation Fund has experts in land acquisition, particularly in navigating its complexity. They step in to acquire at-risk land on behalf of long-term conservation steward partners who may not be able to move quickly enough on their own. The Conservation Fund acts as the acquisition partner, purchasing at-risk lands and then creating a pathway for the conservation partner to eventually buy the land from them" - Justin Nickelson (The Conservation Fund, Georgia) In Atlanta and more broadly across Georgia, the Conservation Fund has supported a number of projects to protect land and green space for the public and incraease land access for farmers. The Conservation Fund works on behalf of city and county partners to purchase land for parks, greenspaces, and trails that will be permanently protected for public use and environmental sustainability, parifcularly through their 'Parks with a Purpose' program in Atlanta (more detail here: https://www.conservationfund.org/our-impact/projects/parks-with-purpose-in-atlanta/). For example, in Atlanta, the Conservation Fund has helped to acquire land for the Browns Mill Food Forest, as well as for the Lake Charlotte Nature Preserve in Southeast Atlanta (216-acres of forested land that would become one of Atlanta's largest protected forests). Read more about the Conservation Fund's work in Atlanta here: https://saportareport.com/the-conservation-fund-making-conservation-work-across-america-and-here-in-atlanta/thought-leadership/the-conservation-fund/ The Conservation Fund is also helping to increase land access for farmers in Georgia, paricularly in the 23 counties surrounding Atlanta, GA. Through the Working Farms Fund Initiative, we secure farmland on the edge of major metro areas and match that farmland to the ideal farmer who leases and stewards the land until TCF protects it forever with an agricultural conservation easement. This is done through a 'Buy-Support-Protect-Sell model', where ultimately the farmer will buy the land back from TCF. Permanently protecting the farm means the land is more affordable for new and growing farm businesses, while keeping it a farm forever. Georgia farms supported by this program include Love is Love Cooperative Farm, Atlanta Harvest, as well as the Rockdale Co-Farm run by the Global Growers Network, among others. Learn more here: https://www.conservationfund.org/our-priorities/working-lands/working-farms/

Small grocery stores were replaced by supermarkets across the county. But too often these new supermarkets were located miles from neighborhoods like South Atlanta. The old stores have had their buildings occupied by other stores. Little Bear, seen here, replaced the Colonial Grocery of the 1950's. Little Bear is not a place where one chooses to go buy their groceries. The corner before Community Grounds and Carver Market! The corner before Community Grounds and Carver Market! In early 2014, we embarked on a fact finding mission in regards to lurring a grocery store to South Atlanta. We found two things: 1) People spend a lot of money on food in our neighborhood, and 2) The amount spent on groceries was not enough for a large national chain to come into our neighborhood anytime soon. While South Atlanta may have had 4 grocery stores at one point, all 4 of them probably could have fit into the frozen food section of a enormous supermarket. We knew by working in South Atlanta since 2001 that access to food was a huge issue. We believe that solving the issue of food access for South Atlantans is critical to returning health and vitality to our community. And so, we started our journey of opening the Carver Neighborhood Market.
